definition: persistently demanding to the point of annoyance
memoryTip: Im-PORTUNE: keep porting the same ask until it’s annoying.
correctPassage: Importunate callers continued to press for an early decision.
wrongPassages: The quiet librarian was importunate, never once interrupting a reader.
She hoped a single polite email would importunate the committee into approval.
His importunate silence filled the room after he refused to speak again.

definition: skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands
memoryTip: Dexterous hands — think “Dexter” building gadgets with skill.
correctPassage: Repairing the mechanism required considerable manual dexterity.
wrongPassages: His verbal dexterity left him tongue-tied and unable to finish a sentence.
They praised her dexterity for dropping every tool she picked up.
The team measured dexterity by how slowly and clumsily the task was done.

definition: without regard to; regardless of
memoryTip: Ir-respective: without respect to X — regardless of it.
correctPassage: The rule applies to all students, irrespective of major.
wrongPassages: Only engineering majors count, irrespective of everyone else’s applications.
She chose the winner with careful respect to rank, calling it irrespective.
His decision was wholly dependent on income, yet labeled irrespective of need.

definition: excessive pride in appearance or achievements
memoryTip: Vain about looks or status — vanity is that excessive pride.
correctPassage: The project was driven more by vanity than by public need.
wrongPassages: Her vanity showed when she credited the whole team and stepped out of the photo.
He treated vanity as pure generosity, giving every award away anonymously.
The modest cabin was built for vanity, with no mirrors and no display of wealth.

definition: not transparent; hard to understand
memoryTip: Can’t see through it — glass that blocks light, or prose that blocks meaning.
correctPassage: The process remains opaque to anyone outside the committee.
wrongPassages: The glass door was so opaque that every desk in the office was clearly visible.
Her opaque summary listed each step in plain language a child could follow.
They called the crystal-clear water opaque because fish swam freely through it.

definition: many and of various types
memoryTip: Multi + farious forms — many varied kinds at once.
correctPassage: Her multifarious interests range from botany to experimental music.
wrongPassages: His multifarious wardrobe held only three identical black shirts.
The museum’s multifarious exhibit featured one painting and nothing else.
They praised the multifarious menu that offered a single soup every day.

definition: arranged in layers; divided into status levels
memoryTip: In strata (layers) — stacked rock or stacked social ranks.
correctPassage: Access to care is stratified by income and geography.
wrongPassages: The town was perfectly stratified: every household earned the same wage.
They mixed the batter until it was stratified into one smooth, even blend.
A stratified seating chart put seniors and freshmen in the exact same rows.

definition: having real importance or a firm basis
memoryTip: Has substance — real weight and importance, not fluff.
correctPassage: The board asked for substantive changes, not cosmetic edits.
wrongPassages: The report was substantive: three bullet points and no evidence at all.
They called the empty apology substantive because it used nice stationery.
A substantive rewrite left every flawed claim untouched and added more filler.

definition: a long step; progress made
memoryTip: A long step forward — or progress (“made great strides”).
correctPassage: Public health has made a significant stride against the disease.
wrongPassages: Progress stalled completely, yet they celebrated a major stride backward.
Her stride across the room was a series of tiny, hesitant shuffles.
Missing every deadline was considered a stride toward the product launch.

definition: proceeding gradually and subtly with harmful effects
memoryTip: In-side-ious: harm sneaks in from inside before you notice.
correctPassage: An insidious form of bias can creep into even careful studies.
wrongPassages: The threat was insidious: a siren blared and every risk was labeled in red.
His insidious honesty left no room for tricks or hidden motives.
They welcomed the insidious improvement that openly fixed every problem overnight.

definition: bring oneself into favor through flattery or effort to please
memoryTip: In + graces: flattery to get into someone’s good graces.
correctPassage: He tried to ingratiate himself with the new director through constant flattery.
wrongPassages: She managed to ingratiate the entire board by insulting each member in turn.
His plan to ingratiate the budget cut was to ignore every request for funding.
They ingratiated the angry crowd by refusing to answer questions at all.

definition: excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters
memoryTip: A garrulous guest pours a garbled river of endless small talk.
correctPassage: A garrulous seatmate made the long flight feel even longer.
wrongPassages: The garrulous hermit went years without speaking to another person.
Her garrulous reply was a single nod and then complete silence.
Judges praised the garrulous witness who answered only yes or no.

definition: intensely enthusiastic or passionate
memoryTip: Fervor on fire — fervid means passion running hot.
correctPassage: Fervid supporters filled the square hours before the speech.
wrongPassages: His fervid reaction was a shrug and a muttered “whatever.”
The crowd stayed fervid by leaving early and barely clapping.
She gave a fervid presentation in a flat monotone that put half the room to sleep.

definition: pressing; demanding immediate attention
memoryTip: Exigent = emergency-urgent — it demands attention now.
correctPassage: Exigent circumstances justified the emergency order.
wrongPassages: The exigent memo could wait until next fiscal year without any harm.
They labeled the optional survey exigent and told staff to ignore it.
His exigent vacation plans involved no deadlines and no time pressure at all.

definition: understood by only a small specialist group
memoryTip: Eso-teric: for the inner circle only — specialist knowledge.
correctPassage: The seminar covers esoteric topics rarely taught to undergraduates.
wrongPassages: The esoteric flyer used words every kindergartner already knew by heart.
They called the national anthem esoteric because the whole stadium sang along.
Her esoteric cooking show explained only how to boil water for pasta.

definition: drain of energy; weaken
memoryTip: E-nerve-ate: strip the nerve/energy out — weaken (not energize!).
correctPassage: Heat and humidity can enervate even seasoned hikers.
wrongPassages: A cold shower and strong coffee will enervate you for the morning run.
The coach’s speech was meant to enervate the team into a furious comeback.
They hoped the rest day would enervate sore muscles back to full strength.

definition: hostile and aggressive
memoryTip: Belli- (war) + gerent — warlike and ready to fight.
correctPassage: A belligerent tone in the letter made negotiation unlikely.
wrongPassages: His belligerent handshake and warm smile put every guest at ease.
The mediator stayed belligerent by refusing to raise her voice or take sides.
They praised the belligerent cease-fire that ended every dispute without a threat.

definition: wanting or devouring great quantities of something
memoryTip: Vora = devour — a huge appetite for food, books, or work.
correctPassage: A voracious reader, she finished several novels each week.
wrongPassages: His voracious appetite was satisfied by half a cracker and a sip of water.
The voracious archive held only one short pamphlet no one ever opened.
She was a voracious student who never finished a single assigned chapter.

definition: a change of circumstances, often unwelcome
memoryTip: Vici-change: the ups and downs fortune throws at you.
correctPassage: The firm survived every vicissitude of the market cycle.
wrongPassages: Life under the monarchy was one long vicissitude of perfect, unchanging calm.
They planned for vicissitude by freezing every policy for the next decade.
The lake’s vicissitude meant the waterline never rose or fell by an inch.

definition: looking or sounding sad and dismal
memoryTip: Lugubrious funeral face — exaggeratedly mournful and gloomy.
correctPassage: A lugubrious soundtrack made the short film feel longer than it was.
wrongPassages: His lugubrious welcome was a bright grin and a round of cheerful jokes.
The parade stayed lugubrious with confetti, brass bands, and dancing crowds.
She delivered a lugubrious toast that left the room laughing for minutes.
